  "title": "Geometric Sensitivity Filtering: Training-Free Velocity-Field Decomposition for Robust Flow-Based Robot Policies Under Geometric Perturbation",
  "core_problem": "Flow-matching and diffusion-based robot policies achieve near-saturated standard benchmark performance (Fast-WAM 97.6% on LIBERO) but are expected to degrade substantially under geometric perturbations based on established findings: LIBERO-Plus demonstrates 95%→<30% drops for strong baselines, and the WAM robustness study (March 2026) identifies geometric perturbation as the dominant failure mode. All existing solutions for geometric robustness require either architectural modification (OA-WAM: object-addressable slots requiring 7B parameter redesign; SDP: SE(3)-equivariant spherical Fourier architecture) or additional training/fine-tuning (CKT-WAM: context knowledge transfer; VGDP: multimodal fusion training; DDP: world model co-training). No training-free, architecture-agnostic inference-time method exists for geometric robustness of pre-trained flow/diffusion policies. The fundamental question: can we improve geometric robustness of ANY pre-trained flow/diffusion policy at test time, without modifying the architecture or retraining? We hypothesize YES, based on a key structural property: flow-matching velocity fields v_θ(a_t, t | o) are DETERMINISTIC functions of their inputs — given a fixed noisy action a_t at timestep t, the velocity is a fixed vector. This means that variance of the velocity field under small geometric augmentations of the observation is PURELY attributable to geometric sensitivity, with no multi-modality confound (unlike ensemble disagreement methods that conflate policy multi-modality with uncertainty). This deterministic property enables clean identification of geometrically-sensitive velocity components via covariance analysis, followed by selective correction using augmentation consensus.",
  "opportunity": "Five converging developments create a precise research opportunity: (1) LIBERO-Plus (2025) and the WAM robustness study (March 2026) establish geometric perturbation as the dominant failure mode, with dramatic performance drops under camera/robot perturbations. The geometric robustness SOTA stands at OA-WAM Camera 80.5%, Robot-Init 89.6% (requires 7B architectural redesign) and CKT-WAM (requires fine-tuning). (2) SE(3)-equivariant approaches (SDP/ICML 2025, EquiBot, ReSeFlow/ICRA 2026, EquiForm 2026) demonstrate geometric equivariance improves robustness — but all require training from scratch. No test-time alternative exists. (3) Inference-time scaling for diffusion/flow models is a validated paradigm (ICLR 2025-2026): noise trajectory search, FK steering, test-time policy composition (GPC/ICLR 2026), and verifier-free test-time sampling (MG-Select/ICLR 2026) all show additional inference compute substitutes for training-time improvements. But none target geometric robustness specifically. (4) DiffStateGrad (ICLR 2025) establishes SVD-based subspace projection as effective for filtering signals in diffusion models, while spectral analysis of diffusion models (NeurIPS 2025) and Gaussian score approximation theory (2024) confirm that score/velocity fields have exploitable low-rank spectral structure. (5) A critical gap in the TTA literature: VOTE (2025) shows prediction averaging improves success (+14.5pp) but smart filtering adds only modest additional improvement (+2.9pp) via trajectory-level cosine voting. However, NO work has exploited the DETERMINISTIC nature of flow-matching velocity fields to perform dimensionwise sensitivity decomposition — a fundamentally different and potentially more powerful approach than trajectory-level ensemble voting. The gap: a principled method leveraging the spectral structure of velocity fields for geometric robustness, applicable to any pre-trained flow/diffusion policy without modification.",
  "landscape": "**Geometric robustness methods (all require training/architecture changes):** OA-WAM (May 2026): object-addressable architecture with per-slot decomposition, Camera 80.5%, Robot 89.6%, Layout 82.8% — requires complete 7B architectural redesign. MG-Select (ICLR 2026): verifier-free test-time sampling via KL-divergence scoring of multiple action candidates — uses sampling diversity not geometric augmentation, not geometric-robustness-specific. VOTE (2025): trajectory ensemble with cosine-similarity voting, Average 61.6% vs Vote 64.5% — trajectory-level voting, not velocity-field-level decomposition. ADPro (2025): manifold-constrained denoising with FGR registration — requires point cloud observations. AnyCamVLA (March 2026): zero-shot camera adaptation via novel view synthesis — VLA-specific, camera-only, requires known camera parameters. TTPL/PDF (April 2026): test-time perturbation learning with augmentation + voting + learned perturbation head, +7.4% on LIBERO — requires episodic environment feedback (delayed reward via REINFORCE); the augmentation+voting component alone is less effective. FK steering (ICLR 2026): Feynman-Kac guided inference — requires explicit reward function. **SVD/spectral methods in diffusion models:** DiffStateGrad (ICLR 2025): SVD projection for image inverse problems — validates low-rank subspace structure in intermediate diffusion states. Spectral Analysis of Diffusion Models (NeurIPS 2025): eigenvalue decomposition reveals coarse-to-fine frequency structure along principal components. Gaussian Score Approximation (2024): scores are well-approximated by low-rank Gaussian models at moderate-to-high noise levels. CPC theory (NeurIPS 2025): CFG implicit decomposition into selective component amplification. All single-modal image settings. **Critical distinction (multi-modality vs. geometric sensitivity):** Diff-DAgger (2024) demonstrates that ensemble disagreement is unreliable for multi-modal diffusion policies because policies disagree at valid multi-modal decision points. However, this concern does NOT apply to velocity-field sensitivity analysis: v_θ(a_t, t | o) is DETERMINISTIC given (a_t, t, o), so variance under geometric augmentation is purely geometric sensitivity, not multi-modal disagreement. This is a fundamental structural advantage of velocity-field-level analysis over trajectory-level ensemble methods. **Gap:** No existing work (1) exploits the deterministic structure of flow-matching velocity fields for clean geometric sensitivity decomposition, (2) proposes selective consensus replacement in high-sensitivity subspaces as an alternative to both suppression and naive averaging, or (3) evaluates such a method on LIBERO-Plus geometric perturbations.",
  "approach": "We propose Geometric Sensitivity Filtering (GSF), a training-free inference-time method that improves geometric robustness of pre-trained flow-matching/diffusion robot policies by decomposing velocity fields into geometrically-stable and geometrically-sensitive subspaces, then selectively applying augmentation consensus in the sensitive subspace while preserving nominal precision in the stable subspace.\n\n**Key Theoretical Insight: Why This Differs From Ensemble Methods.** Flow-matching velocity fields v_θ(a_t, t | o) are deterministic functions: given a fixed noisy action a_t at integration step t with observation o, the output is a single vector with no stochasticity. This means that when we compute velocity fields from geometrically-augmented observations {T_k(o)}, ALL variance across the K augmented velocity fields is attributable to geometric sensitivity — there is no multi-modality confound. This distinguishes GSF from ensemble/disagreement methods (e.g., Diff-DAgger shows ensemble variance conflates multi-modality with uncertainty at the trajectory level). At the velocity-field level with fixed (a_t, t), the analysis is clean.\n\n**Why GSF Beats Simple Averaging (The Core Technical Argument).** Consider three alternatives at each integration step:\n- Nominal only: v_0 = v_θ(a_t, t | o) — uses unreliable velocity components when o is geometrically shifted from training distribution\n- Simple TTA (full average): v̄ = (1/K)Σ v_k — treats ALL dimensions equally, diluting precision in stable dimensions (where nominal is reliable) while gaining robustness in sensitive dimensions\n- GSF (selective consensus): uses v_0 in low-sensitivity dimensions (preserving maximum precision where the velocity field is locally stable) and v̄ in high-sensitivity dimensions (improving robustness where the velocity field is unreliable)\n\nGSF dominates both alternatives: it preserves nominal precision where possible (unlike TTA averaging) while improving robustness where needed (unlike nominal-only). The SVD identifies the decomposition boundary — it's not arbitrary but determined by the actual sensitivity structure at each (a_t, t).\n\n**Phased Research Plan with Explicit Gates:**\n\n**Phase 0 — Spectral Diagnostic (1 day, ~2-3h H100).** Before committing to full development: take 5-10 LIBERO-Plus camera-perturbed episodes, compute velocity fields from 8 small geometric augmentations at several integration steps, compute the eigenvalue spectrum of the velocity covariance. GATE: If the spectrum is flat (ratio of top to bottom eigenvalue < 3), there is no exploitable structure and GSF cannot work — abort. If there is a clear spectral gap (top 2-3 eigenvalues dominate, >10x ratio), proceed. Expected outcome: based on DiffStateGrad's findings of clear low-rank structure in diffusion states and established spectral structure theory, we expect a gap — but this must be verified.\n\n**Phase 1 — Fast-WAM LIBERO-Plus Baseline (2-3 days, ~10-15h H100).** Evaluate Fast-WAM's released checkpoint on LIBERO-Plus Camera L1/L3 and Robot-Init L1/L3, 20 episodes each. GATE: If Fast-WAM maintains >85% (unlikely given LIBERO-Plus findings), the improvement ceiling is too small. If it drops to 40-70%, there is substantial room for GSF. If <40%, absolute numbers may be too low to be competitive regardless of relative improvement — consider switching backbone to OA-WAM if checkpoint becomes available.\n\n**Phase 2 — GSF Implementation and Evaluation (8-12 days).**\n\n**Core Mechanism.** At each integration step t during inference:\n1. Given current observation o and noisy action a_t, compute the nominal velocity: v_0 = v_θ(a_t, t | o)\n2. Generate K=4-6 small geometric augmentations of the observation: {T_k(o)} where T_k are random camera jitter (±2-4° rotation, ±3-5% translation) and/or spatial crops\n3. Compute augmented velocities: v_k = v_θ(a_t, t | T_k(o)) for k=1,...,K\n4. Compute velocity covariance across augmentations: C_t = (1/K) Σ_k (v_k - v̄)(v_k - v̄)^T where v̄ = (1/K)Σ v_k\n5. SVD of C_t = U_t Λ_t U_t^T. Top eigenvectors (high eigenvalues) = high geometric sensitivity directions\n6. Construct subspace decomposition: Π_high = Σ_{i: λ_i > τ·tr(Λ)} u_i u_i^T, Π_low = I - Π_high\n7. Apply selective consensus: v_filtered = Π_low · v_0 + Π_high · v̄\n8. Use v_filtered for the integration step\n\n**Interpretation:** In low-sensitivity directions (Π_low), we trust the nominal velocity v_0 computed from the actual (shifted) observation — it retains full precision for stable components. In high-sensitivity directions (Π_high), we replace the unreliable nominal with the augmentation consensus v̄ — which averages out the geometric-sensitivity-induced variability, providing a more robust (if less precise) estimate.\n\n**Adaptive Integration Schedule.** Early integration steps (high noise/far from data) determine coarse trajectory structure and are most geometry-dependent; later steps refine timing and precision. Apply GSF with adaptive strength: aggressive decomposition (lower τ, larger Π_high) at early steps, conservative (higher τ, smaller Π_high) at later steps. Based on the spectral analysis finding that low-rank approximation quality decreases with noise level, we apply full GSF at steps 1-4 (of 10) and nominal-only at steps 5-10, with linear interpolation for the threshold.\n\n**Computational Overhead.** GSF requires K+1 forward passes per filtered integration step. For K=4, applying GSF at M=4 of T=10 steps: 4×5 + 6×1 = 26 forward passes vs. 10 baseline — 2.6x overhead. Optimizations: (i) Cache visual backbone features across integration steps (the observation doesn't change; only recompute action-expert forward pass). (ii) For Fast-WAM's MoT architecture, the video DiT backbone (5B) is shared; only the 1B action expert needs K+1 passes. With feature caching, effective overhead is ~1.5-2x on wall-clock time.\n\n**Backbone Strategy.** Primary: Fast-WAM (97.6% standard LIBERO, released code + HuggingFace checkpoints, flow-matching action head with 10 integration steps, MoT architecture with video DiT + action expert DiT). Secondary: Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., diffusion-based, widely used). Extension: demonstrate on a non-WAM architecture (e.g., standard Diffusion Policy or a VLA with diffusion/flow head) to validate architecture-agnosticism.\n\n**Evaluation Strategy.** Primary benchmark: LIBERO-Plus geometric perturbations — Camera (L1, L3) and Robot-Init (L1, L3), plus Light as control (non-geometric, expect no benefit or slight degradation). Standard LIBERO as sanity check (expect 1-3% degradation from information loss in filtered components). \n\nBaselines: (i) Fast-WAM standard inference (nominal only), (ii) Fast-WAM + Simple TTA: average K+1 velocity fields uniformly then integrate (same compute budget as GSF — the critical apples-to-apples comparison), (iii) Fast-WAM + VOTE-style action voting: generate K+1 full trajectories and select by consensus, (iv) Fast-WAM + GSF (ours — selective consensus in sensitivity-decomposed subspace). \n\nAblations: (a) filtering threshold τ ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5} as fraction of trace, (b) number of augmentations K ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8}, (c) augmentation type and magnitude, (d) adaptive vs. uniform schedule across integration steps, (e) which integration steps to apply GSF, (f) eigenvalue spectrum visualization across tasks/perturbation types, (g) component analysis: what do high-sensitivity directions encode? (visualize by perturbing actions along top eigenvectors and rendering predicted trajectories).\n\n**Framing vs. Competitors:** GSF is positioned as a lightweight inference-time method for improving geometric robustness of pre-trained flow/diffusion policies, complementary to training-time approaches. It requires only K+1 forward passes at selected integration steps and no architectural modification. It is NOT equivalent to SE(3)-equivariant methods (which achieve exact mathematical equivariance); rather, it provides approximate geometric stability via empirical sensitivity analysis. The key advantages over alternatives: vs. OA-WAM/CKT-WAM — no retraining/redesign needed; vs. TTPL/PDF — no environment feedback required; vs. AnyCamVLA — no camera parameter knowledge needed, handles robot-init perturbation too; vs. simple TTA — exploits directional sensitivity structure rather than treating all dimensions equally.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 8)
Issues: ["AUGMENTATION-PERTURBATION MAGNITUDE GAP (HIGH RISK): GSF uses ±2-4° rotation, ±3-5% translation as augmentations to probe local sensitivity. LIBERO-Plus camera perturbations are much larger (L1-L5 graduated levels with substantial viewpoint shifts). The first-order sensitivity structure at the nominal observation (computed from small augmentations) may not predict which velocity directions fail under large perturbations. A velocity component that is locally stable (low sensitivity to ±3°) could become catastrophically unstable at ±15°. The proposal should discuss this gap and either (a) include augmentation magnitude as a key hyperparameter sweep, or (b) argue theoretically why local sensitivity is predictive of large-perturbation failure modes.", "GSF VS SIMPLE TTA THEORETICAL GAP: The argument that GSF dominates simple TTA is intuitive but lacks formal analysis. Simple TTA averages ALL dimensions uniformly; GSF preserves nominal precision in stable dimensions. But in robot manipulation, spatial precision IS the task — the 'stable' dimensions (low geometric sensitivity) may encode precisely the task-relevant spatial information that should NOT be filtered. If geometric perturbation primarily causes errors in 'semantically important' dimensions rather than 'geometrically sensitive' dimensions, GSF's filtering criterion is misaligned. The proposal needs a concrete example or formal bias-variance decomposition showing when GSF's criterion aligns with task relevance.", "FALLBACK IF GSF ≈ SIMPLE TTA IS MISSING: The gated plan handles Phase 0 failure (flat spectrum → abort) and Phase 1 failure (insufficient baseline degradation → abort). But there is no explicit gate for the most probable failure mode: GSF provides marginal improvement over simple TTA (<2-3pp). If the spectral gap exists and augmentation helps, but SVD-based selection doesn't meaningfully outperform uniform averaging, the paper reduces to 'TTA helps flow policies under perturbation' — which is not novel enough for CoRL as a method paper.", "SPECTRAL ANALYSIS EVIDENCE IS FROM WRONG DOMAIN: The proposal cites DiffStateGrad (image restoration), Spectral Analysis of Diffusion Models (NeurIPS 2025, image generation), and Gaussian Score Approximation (image scores) as evidence that exploitable spectral structure exists. However, my verification confirms these papers analyze score functions in IMAGE domains, not velocity fields in ROBOT ACTION domains. Robot action velocity fields operate in a fundamentally different space (7-14D joint/end-effector actions vs 64×64×3 images). The low-rank spectral structure hypothesis may not transfer. Phase 0 correctly tests this, but the proposal overstates the prior evidence.", "TIMELINE RISK — NO BUFFER FOR PAPER WRITING: The phased plan fills 16 days (Phase 0: day 1, Phase 1: days 2-4, Phase 2: days 5-16). Abstract deadline is May 26 (day 16), paper deadline May 29 (day 19). This leaves zero days for unexpected issues in Phase 2 and only 3 days for paper writing after completing all experiments. Realistic paper writing for an 8-page CoRL paper with figures, tables, and ablation analysis takes 3-5 days minimum, meaning Phase 2 must complete by day 14 at latest."]
Feedback: The proposal has improved dramatically across 7 rounds and is now very close to pass quality. The core mechanism (velocity-field decomposition via SVD + selective consensus) is genuinely novel and well-motivated. To reach pass in the next round:

**1. ADDRESS THE AUGMENTATION-PERTURBATION MAGNITUDE GAP:** Add a concrete argument for why local sensitivity (±3° augmentation) predicts large-perturbation failure. Hypothesis: the velocity field's sensitivity directions are approximately invariant to perturbation magnitude (the DIRECTIONS of high sensitivity are stable even as magnitudes change) — the SVD identifies WHICH dimensions are geometry-dependent, not HOW MUCH they change. This is testable in Phase 0 by computing SVD at multiple augmentation magnitudes and checking cosine similarity of top eigenvectors. Include this as a Phase 0 diagnostic.

**2. ADD A FORMAL ARGUMENT FOR GSF > SIMPLE TTA:** Frame the comparison as a bias-variance tradeoff. Let v_0 be the nominal velocity (low bias, high variance in sensitive directions under perturbation). Let v̄ be the TTA mean (lower variance everywhere, but biased — it averages over augmented observations that don't match the actual scene). GSF achieves the best of both: v_0 in stable dimensions (low bias, low variance) and v̄ in sensitive dimensions (moderate bias, low variance). The key claim: v_0's variance in sensitive directions under real perturbation exceeds v̄'s bias in those same directions. If you can argue this (even heuristically), the advantage is clear.

**3. ADD AN EXPLICIT GATE FOR GSF-VS-TTA:** Include a Phase 2 decision point: after running GSF and simple TTA on Camera L1 (the easiest perturbation condition) with 20 episodes, compare. ## Detailed Research Findings

### 1. LIBERO-Plus Perturbation Magnitudes (L1-L5)

**Paper:** Sylvest et al., "LIBERO-Plus: In-depth Robustness Analysis of Vision-Language-Action Models" ([arXiv:2510.13626](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13626))

**Critical finding: L1-L5 are NOT defined by perturbation magnitude.** They are defined by model performance:
- **L1**: Solved by all four reference models
- **L2**: Solved by exactly three models
- **L3**: Solved by exactly two models
- **L4**: Solved by exactly one model
- **L5**: Solved by none

The actual camera perturbation ranges are specified as three sub-dimensions with continuous ranges (Section A.4):
- **C1 -- Camera Distance**: 1.01x to 2.00x the original value (camera moved along optical axis)
- **C2 -- Spherical Position**: Azimuth and elevation perturbed within 15 to 75 degree cones
- **C3 -- Camera Orientation**: Yaw, pitch, and roll perturbed within 2 to 10 degrees

This is important for your proposal: the L1-L5 labels do NOT correspond to progressively larger perturbation magnitudes. A given perturbation magnitude may land in different difficulty levels depending on which task and which geometric sub-dimension it applies to. A 20-degree azimuth shift might be L2 for one task but L5 for another. This actually strengthens the case for GSF, because it means that the relevant question is not "how big is the perturbation" but "which dimensions is the policy sensitive to" -- exactly what GSF probes.

Performance drops are severe: from 95% to below 30% under "modest" camera perturbations. The benchmark includes 10,030 tasks across 7 perturbation dimensions and 21 sub-dimensions.

---

### 2. Whether Local Sensitivity Predicts Behavior Under Large Perturbations

This is the key theoretical challenge for GSF. The evidence is nuanced:

**Evidence SUPPORTING local-to-large transfer (directional consistency):**

- **Singular-vector alignment in deep Jacobians** ([arXiv:2602.12384](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.12384v2)): Theorem 6.1 proves that strong spectral separation in matrix products forces dominant singular vectors to align. The dominant left singular subspace of intermediate Jacobians converges to that of the full Jacobian. This means the *directions* of maximal input-output sensitivity remain approximately constant even as singular values (magnitudes) change exponentially. This is measured quantitatively via diagonal correlation coefficients showing concentration around the diagonal.

- **"Beyond Activation Alignment" paper** ([arXiv:2605.03222](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.03222)): Section 4.2 shows that local sensitivity directions (found via infinitesimal Jacobian analysis) do transfer to finite perturbation regimes. "Contrast-derived perturbations instantiated as finite image deformations" transfer to held-out images and models, achieving separations of 1.10 vs controls. However, the authors explicitly note their framework is "local, dataset-level, and second-moment based" and "does not capture strongly nonlinear finite-perturbation behavior."

- **Adversarial gradient direction consistency**: MI-FGSM research shows that accumulated gradient directions from previous steps guide adversarial perturbations in a "more consistent direction" that transfers across models. Robust models have gradients better aligned with class-centroid vectors than non-robust models, and this alignment is a structural property not dependent on perturbation magnitude.

- **Adversarial transferability via Jacobian SVD** ([Springer: Applied Intelligence](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10489-022-04066-2)): The singular vectors of the Jacobian "define the possible local optimal solutions of perturbations" and the singular matrix describes the model's adversarial distribution. The maximum singular value defines maximum output variation under L2 norm.

**Evidence AGAINST or LIMITING local-to-large transfer:**

- **Taylor expansion breakdown**: Linearized approximations (the Jacobian is a first-order Taylor expansion) are valid only when perturbations are small and data is concentrated around the expansion point. For larger perturbations, higher-order terms dominate. This is well-established theoretically.

- **Robustness crossover**: Differential attention research ([arXiv:2510.00517](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00517v2)) shows a perturbation-dependent trade-off: sensitivity patterns at small epsilon (1/255) differ qualitatively from those at larger epsilon (4/255). Negative gradient alignment amplifies sensitivity at small perturbations but this effect diminishes at larger scales.

- **Adversarial attack direction evolution**: Research on misclassification of robust networks found that "previous attacks under-explore the perturbation space during optimization, leading to unsuccessful attacks for samples where the initial gradient direction is not a good approximation of the final adversarial perturbation direction." This suggests that for some inputs, the direction found at small scale does NOT predict the optimal perturbation direction at large scale.

**Synthesis for your proposal:** The strongest evidence you can cite is the singular-vector alignment theorem (arXiv:2602.12384), which provides a rigorous mathematical basis for the claim that WHICH dimensions are sensitive (the singular vectors) remains stable even as HOW MUCH they are sensitive (the singular values) changes. This is exactly the "sensitivity direction invariance" property GSF relies on. You should acknowledge the Taylor expansion limitation but argue that GSF needs only directional consistency (which dimensions are most sensitive), not magnitude accuracy (how much the output changes).

---

### 3. Sensitivity Direction Invariance

The concept you describe -- that WHICH dimensions are sensitive stays consistent across perturbation magnitudes even if HOW MUCH they change varies -- has strong theoretical support but is not yet named "sensitivity direction invariance" in the literature. The closest concepts are:

- **Singular-vector alignment** (arXiv:2602.12384): Theorem 6.1 proves that dominant singular vectors of the Jacobian converge to a shared basis. The paper proves "singular directions stabilize" under spectral separation, with the rotation matrix R_L converging to identity. A small number of input directions capture most output sensitivity consistently.

- **Structural gradient alignment** (arXiv:2510.00517): Negative gradient alignment is shown to be a "structural property rather than an anomaly" -- the alignment pattern persists across layers and is a feature of architecture, not of perturbation magnitude.

- **Lipschitz-based sensitivity bounds**: The Lipschitz constant provides an upper bound on output change relative to input change. While this bounds magnitude, the directions that achieve the bound (the top singular vectors) are structurally determined by the network weights, not by perturbation size.

- **Invariance-sensitivity tradeoffs** ([arXiv:2002.04599](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04599)): Trotta et al. establish that "excessively invariant classifiers" arise from "overly-robust predictive features in standard datasets," suggesting the invariance/sensitivity profile is a structural property of the learned representation.

This body of work supports the argument that GSF's small-perturbation probes can identify the sensitive dimensions, and those dimensions will remain the sensitive ones under larger perturbations -- even if the response magnitude is nonlinear.

---

### 4. Test-Time Augmentation Magnitude Selection

- **MEMO** ([arXiv:2110.09506](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.09506)): Performs diverse augmentations at test time and adapts model parameters by minimizing entropy of the average output distribution across augmentations. Achieves 1-8% accuracy gains. Does not explicitly address augmentation magnitude selection.

- **Adaptive Sensitivity Analysis for Robust Augmentation** ([arXiv:2406.01425](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.01425)): This is the most directly relevant work. They define sensitivity as "the ratio of the change in model accuracy to the change in KID (Kernel Inception Distance)" and solve an optimization to find perturbation levels where "small changes in augmentation lead to large changes in model performance." They use PCHIP spline interpolation to adaptively estimate the sensitivity curve during training, then select augmentation intensities at equal intervals along this curve. This is 10x faster and 200x less storage than prior methods. The key insight: they don't uniformly sample augmentation magnitudes -- they concentrate on magnitudes where the model is most sensitive.

- **GenSplat** ([arXiv:2603.29192](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29192)): Uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to synthesize novel camera views for robotic policy training augmentation. Specifically designed for camera pose augmentation in policy learning, ensuring "robust execution under severe spatial perturbations."

- **Diffusion policy noise rescaling**: Recent work on diffusion policies for robot manipulation found that "the increase in score resulting from using lower noise scales is significant" -- the same model can substantially improve task success rates with noise rescaling at test time, suggesting that augmentation magnitude at test time is a critical hyperparameter.

1. **arXiv:2602.12384** -- "Why Deep Jacobian Spectra Separate: Depth-Induced Scaling and Singular-Vector Alignment" -- Theorem 6.1 proving singular-vector alignment (the strongest theoretical support)

The actual camera perturbation ranges are specified as three sub-dimensions with continuous ranges (Section A.4):
- **C1 -- Camera Distance**: 1.01x to 2.00x the original value (camera moved along optical axis)
- **C2 -- Spherical Position**: Azimuth and elevation perturbed within 15 to 75 degree cones
- **C3 -- Camera Orientation**: Yaw, pitch, and roll perturbed within 2 to 10 degrees

This is important for your proposal: the L1-L5 labels do NOT correspond to progressively larger perturbation magnitudes. A given perturbation magnitude may land in different difficulty levels depending on which task and which geometric sub-dimension it applies to. A 20-degree azimuth shift might be L2 for one task but L5 for another. This actually strengthens the case for GSF, because it means that the relevant question is not "how big is the perturbation" but "which dimensions is the policy sensitive to" -- exactly what GSF probes.

Performance drops are severe: from 95% to below 30% under "modest" camera perturbations. The benchmark includes 10,030 tasks across 7 perturbation dimensions and 21 sub-dimensions.

---

### 2. Whether Local Sensitivity Predicts Behavior Under Large Perturbations

This is the key theoretical challenge for GSF. The evidence is nuanced:

**Evidence SUPPORTING local-to-large transfer (directional consistency):**

- **Singular-vector alignment in deep Jacobians** ([arXiv:2602.12384](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.12384v2)): Theorem 6.1 proves that strong spectral separation in matrix products forces dominant singular vectors to align. The dominant left singular subspace of intermediate Jacobians converges to that of the full Jacobian. This means the *directions* of maximal input-output sensitivity remain approximately constant even as singular values (magnitudes) change exponentially. This is measured quantitatively via diagonal correlation coefficients showing concentration around the diagonal.

- **"Beyond Activation Alignment" paper** ([arXiv:2605.03222](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.03222)): Section 4.2 shows that local sensitivity directions (found via infinitesimal Jacobian analysis) do transfer to finite perturbation regimes. "Contrast-derived perturbations instantiated as finite image deformations" transfer to held-out images and models, achieving separations of 1.10 vs controls. However, the authors explicitly note their framework is "local, dataset-level, and second-moment based" and "does not capture strongly nonlinear finite-perturbation behavior."

- **Adversarial gradient direction consistency**: MI-FGSM research shows that accumulated gradient directions from previous steps guide adversarial perturbations in a "more consistent direction" that transfers across models. Robust models have gradients better aligned with class-centroid vectors than non-robust models, and this alignment is a structural property not dependent on perturbation magnitude.

- **Adversarial transferability via Jacobian SVD** ([Springer: Applied Intelligence](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10489-022-04066-2)): The singular vectors of the Jacobian "define the possible local optimal solutions of perturbations" and the singular matrix describes the model's adversarial distribution. The maximum singular value defines maximum output variation under L2 norm.

**Evidence AGAINST or LIMITING local-to-large transfer:**

- **Taylor expansion breakdown**: Linearized approximations (the Jacobian is a first-order Taylor expansion) are valid only when perturbations are small and data is concentrated around the expansion point. For larger perturbations, higher-order terms dominate. This is well-established theoretically.

- **Robustness crossover**: Differential attention research ([arXiv:2510.00517](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00517v2)) shows a perturbation-dependent trade-off: sensitivity patterns at small epsilon (1/255) differ qualitatively from those at larger epsilon (4/255). Negative gradient alignment amplifies sensitivity at small perturbations but this effect diminishes at larger scales.

- **Adversarial attack direction evolution**: Research on misclassification of robust networks found that "previous attacks under-explore the perturbation space during optimization, leading to unsuccessful attacks for samples where the initial gradient direction is not a good approximation of the final adversarial perturbation direction." This suggests that for some inputs, the direction found at small scale does NOT predict the optimal perturbation direction at large scale.

**Synthesis for your proposal:** The strongest evidence you can cite is the singular-vector alignment theorem (arXiv:2602.12384), which provides a rigorous mathematical basis for the claim that WHICH dimensions are sensitive (the singular vectors) remains stable even as HOW MUCH they are sensitive (the singular values) changes. This is exactly the "sensitivity direction invariance" property GSF relies on. You should acknowledge the Taylor expansion limitation but argue that GSF needs only directional consistency (which dimensions are most sensitive), not magnitude accuracy (how much the output changes).

---

### 3. Sensitivity Direction Invariance

The concept you describe -- that WHICH dimensions are sensitive stays consistent across perturbation magnitudes even if HOW MUCH they change varies -- has strong theoretical support but is not yet named "sensitivity direction invariance" in the literature. The closest concepts are:

- **Singular-vector alignment** (arXiv:2602.12384): Theorem 6.1 proves that dominant singular vectors of the Jacobian converge to a shared basis. The paper proves "singular directions stabilize" under spectral separation, with the rotation matrix R_L converging to identity. A small number of input directions capture most output sensitivity consistently.

- **Structural gradient alignment** (arXiv:2510.00517): Negative gradient alignment is shown to be a "structural property rather than an anomaly" -- the alignment pattern persists across layers and is a feature of architecture, not of perturbation magnitude.

- **Lipschitz-based sensitivity bounds**: The Lipschitz constant provides an upper bound on output change relative to input change. While this bounds magnitude, the directions that achieve the bound (the top singular vectors) are structurally determined by the network weights, not by perturbation size.

- **Invariance-sensitivity tradeoffs** ([arXiv:2002.04599](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04599)): Trotta et al. establish that "excessively invariant classifiers" arise from "overly-robust predictive features in standard datasets," suggesting the invariance/sensitivity profile is a structural property of the learned representation.

This body of work supports the argument that GSF's small-perturbation probes can identify the sensitive dimensions, and those dimensions will remain the sensitive ones under larger perturbations -- even if the response magnitude is nonlinear.

---

### 4. Test-Time Augmentation Magnitude Selection

- **MEMO** ([arXiv:2110.09506](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.09506)): Performs diverse augmentations at test time and adapts model parameters by minimizing entropy of the average output distribution across augmentations. Achieves 1-8% accuracy gains. Does not explicitly address augmentation magnitude selection.

- **Adaptive Sensitivity Analysis for Robust Augmentation** ([arXiv:2406.01425](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.01425)): This is the most directly relevant work. They define sensitivity as "the ratio of the change in model accuracy to the change in KID (Kernel Inception Distance)" and solve an optimization to find perturbation levels where "small changes in augmentation lead to large changes in model performance." They use PCHIP spline interpolation to adaptively estimate the sensitivity curve during training, then select augmentation intensities at equal intervals along this curve. This is 10x faster and 200x less storage than prior methods. The key insight: they don't uniformly sample augmentation magnitudes -- they concentrate on magnitudes where the model is most sensitive.

- **GenSplat** ([arXiv:2603.29192](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29192)): Uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to synthesize novel camera views for robotic policy training augmentation. Specifically designed for camera pose augmentation in policy learning, ensuring "robust execution under severe spatial perturbations."

- **Diffusion policy noise rescaling**: Recent work on diffusion policies for robot manipulation found that "the increase in score resulting from using lower noise scales is significant" -- the same model can substantially improve task success rates with noise rescaling at test time, suggesting that augmentation magnitude at test time is a critical hyperparameter.

---

### Summary of Key Citations for Your Proposal

For the argument that GSF's small-perturbation probes predict large-perturbation sensitivity DIRECTIONS:

1. **arXiv:2602.12384** -- "Why Deep Jacobian Spectra Separate: Depth-Induced Scaling and Singular-Vector Alignment" -- Theorem 6.1 proving singular-vector alignment (the strongest theoretical support)

I now have comprehensive findings across all three topics. Here is the detailed research report.

---

## RESEARCH FINDINGS REPORT

---

### TOPIC 1: Bias-Variance Decomposition for Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) Methods

I found several highly relevant papers that provide formal theoretical foundations you can use to argue that selective consensus (GSF) outperforms simple averaging (TTA).

#### 1A. "Understanding Test-Time Augmentation" -- Kimura (2024)

This is the most directly relevant paper. It provides:

- **Theorem 3.1**: The expected error of TTA is bounded from above by the average error of individual predictions. TTA cannot perform worse than the average individual model when the transformation class contains the identity.
- **Theorem 3.2**: When individual errors have zero mean and are uncorrelated, TTA achieves a factor-of-m improvement: R_TTA = (1/m) * R_avg. This is the best case for uniform averaging.
- **Proposition 2 (Ambiguity Decomposition)**: The TTA error decomposes as: R_TTA = [weighted average of individual errors] - [ambiguity term]. The ambiguity term measures prediction diversity. *Higher ambiguity (diverse predictions) benefits TTA; correlated predictions provide minimal gains.* This is critical for your argument -- if some dimensions have low ambiguity (high correlation across augmentations), averaging them adds noise without reducing error.
- **Theorem 3.3 (Optimal Weights)**: The closed-form optimal weights use the inverse covariance matrix of prediction errors: w_i = (sum_j Gamma^{-1}_{ij}) / (sum_k sum_j Gamma^{-1}_{kj}). The authors note the correlation matrix among augmented predictions is often near-singular, making uniform weights suboptimal. This directly supports dimension-wise weighting.

**Key argument for GSF**: Theorem 3.3 shows optimal aggregation requires *non-uniform* weights determined by the error covariance structure. GSF's dimension-selective consensus can be seen as a sparse approximation of this optimal weighting -- averaging only in dimensions where the ambiguity term is large (high sensitivity) and preserving the original prediction in dimensions where augmentations are redundant.

Paper: [Understanding Test-Time Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06892)

#### 1B. "Better Aggregation in Test-Time Augmentation" -- Shanmugam et al. (ICCV 2021)

Key findings:
- Even when TTA produces a net improvement, it changes many correct predictions into incorrect ones. Uniform averaging is demonstrably suboptimal.
- They propose a *learned weighting matrix* for aggregating TTA predictions that minimizes validation loss.
- Consistent improvements over uniform averaging across diverse models, datasets, and augmentations.

This empirically validates that dimension-wise or sample-wise selective aggregation beats uniform averaging.

Paper: [Better Aggregation in Test-Time Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.11156) (ICCV 2021)

#### 1C. "A Group-Theoretic Framework for Data Augmentation" -- Chen, Dobriban, Lee (JMLR 2020, NeurIPS 2020)

Key theoretical results:
- Data augmentation is formally equivalent to **averaging over group orbits**, which reduces variance.
- **Invariance-variance tradeoff**: Orbit averaging reduces variance, but introduces bias when the true function is not exactly invariant. The bias term vanishes under exact invariance.
- **Formal result**: The bias of the augmented estimator equals the original bias, and the covariance matrix *decreases in the Loewner order*, hence MSE decreases.

**Key argument for GSF**: This framework shows that averaging helps *only along directions where the function has approximate invariance*. In dimensions where the function is NOT invariant to the augmentation group, averaging introduces bias. GSF's selective consensus naturally restricts averaging to dimensions with approximate invariance (low geometric sensitivity), avoiding the bias penalty in non-invariant dimensions.

Paper: [A Group-Theoretic Framework for Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10905) (JMLR Vol 21, 2020)

#### 1D. "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly Sides of Data Augmentation" -- Lin et al. (JMLR 2024)

Key findings:
- DA induces *implicit spectral regularization* through two effects: (1) manipulating relative eigenvalue proportions of the data covariance matrix, and (2) uniformly boosting the entire spectrum (equivalent to ridge regression).
- Demonstrates that augmentation can *hurt* in certain regimes ("the ugly side"), particularly when the spectral manipulation misaligns with the signal structure.
- The framework reveals discrepancies between overparameterized and underparameterized regimes.

**Key argument for GSF**: This paper shows augmentation's benefit depends on alignment between the augmentation's spectral effect and the signal's spectral structure. In robot action spaces where different dimensions have different spectral properties, uniform augmentation/averaging across all dimensions creates spectral misalignment. GSF's dimension-selective approach avoids this.

Paper: [The Good, the Bad and the Ugly Sides of Data Augmentation](https://jmlr.org/papers/v25/22-1312.html) (JMLR Vol 25, 2024)

#### 1E. "Efficient Improvement of Classification Accuracy via Selective Test-Time Augmentation" (Information Sciences, 2023)

Proposes selective TTA that quantifies predictive uncertainty to determine *whether* TTA should be performed, applying it only when uncertainty is high. This reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy. Selective aggregation based on risk/reward criteria reduces bias from abnormal transformations.

Paper: [Selective Test-Time Augmentation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0020025523007338) (Information Sciences, 2023)

---

### TOPIC 2: Spectral Structure in Robot Action Spaces

I found strong evidence that robot action spaces exhibit spectral structure (low-rank, low-frequency dominance), drawn from ROBOTICS domains rather than images.

#### 2A. FreqPolicy -- (2025, arXiv 2506.01583)

This is the strongest single paper for your needs. It provides direct empirical analysis of spectral structure in robot action spaces:

- **Key finding**: The first 30% of frequency bands preserves 95% of signal energy in robot actions.
- Most energy concentrates in the 0-10% low-frequency bands across both high-DoF (26-DoF Adroit hand) and low-DoF (10-DoF Robomimic gripper) tasks.
- Simple tasks (pick-and-place) maintain performance with only 12% of low-frequency content preserved.
- Complex dexterous tasks require more frequency components.
- "Low-frequency components reflect global movement patterns, while high-frequency components encode fine local details."
- Uses Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) analysis on Adroit and Robomimic benchmarks.

**This directly supports the GSF assumption** that robot action spaces have spectral structure where different frequency bands carry different amounts of information.

Paper: [FreqPolicy: Frequency Autoregressive Visuomotor Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01583) (2025)

#### 2B. Santello, Flanders, Soechting -- "Postural Hand Synergies for Tool Use" (J. Neuroscience, 1998)

The landmark paper on hand synergies:
- PCA of 15 hand joint angles during grasping shows the **first 2 principal components explain >80% of variance**.
- Higher-order components are not random noise but carry object-specific information.
- This is a foundational result showing low-rank structure in manipulation-relevant action spaces.

Paper: [Postural Hand Synergies for Tool Use](https://www.jneurosci.org/content/18/23/10105) (J. Neuroscience, 1998)

#### 2C. PCHands -- PCA-based Hand Pose Synergy Representation (2025, arXiv 2508.07945)

- Demonstrates that **2 principal components are typically sufficient** for learning complex dexterous manipulation tasks on hands with 16, 9, and 18 DoF.
- The first principal component universally encodes hand opening/closing across all 16 tested manipulator morphologies.
- Performance with 1-2 PCs was "predominantly better than 4-pc" in demonstration-augmented learning.

Paper: [PCHands: PCA-based Hand Pose Synergy Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07945) (2025)

#### 2D. PCA-Based Algorithms for Humanoid Robot Motion Behavior (Int. J. Humanoid Robotics, 2015)

- Uses PCA to find synergies in humanoid robot motion.
- Demonstrates that robot motion trajectories can be efficiently represented using a small number of principal components.

Paper: [PCA-Based Algorithms to Find Synergies for Humanoid Robot Motion](https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0219843615500371)

#### 2E. "Exploiting Upper-Limb Functional Principal Components" (Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 2020)

Directly relevant empirical results:
- **More than 80% of variance explained by only 3 functional principal components** for robot arm trajectories.
- The first component alone accounts for 96% of cost reduction in trajectory optimization.
- Free-motion tasks need only 1 PC; single-obstacle scenarios need 2; double-obstacle needs 3.
- Lower-order PCs contribute low-frequency motion, higher-order PCs add high-frequency detail -- directly paralleling the frequency-domain analysis in FreqPolicy.

Paper: [Exploiting Upper-Limb Functional Principal Components](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7218840/) (2020)

#### 2F. EigenTrajectory -- Low-Rank Descriptors for Multi-Modal Trajectory Forecasting (ICCV 2023)

- Uses SVD decomposition on trajectory data, demonstrating strong low-rank structure.
- **k=6 eigenvectors** effectively represent trajectory space (originally 2*T dimensional).
- First two eigenvectors encode constant-velocity motion; subsequent ones capture velocity changes and fine details.
- Eigenvalue spectrum shows rapid decay, confirming low-rank structure.

Paper: [EigenTrajectory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09306) (ICCV 2023)

#### 2G. Dimensionality Reduction for Probabilistic Movement Primitives (2015)

- The intrinsic dimensionality of human/robot movements is small compared to the number of DoF.
- Dimensionality reduction applied to ProMPs preserves essential trajectory information.

Paper: [Dimensionality Reduction for Probabilistic Movement Primitives](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/283882361_Dimensionality_reduction_for_probabilistic_movement_primitives) (2015)

#### 2H. "Learning Latent Actions to Control Assistive Robots" (Autonomous Robots, 2021)

- Demonstrates that 7-DoF robot arm control can be compressed to **1-2 latent dimensions** while preserving task-relevant structure.
- Even complex manipulation tasks (reaching, cutting, scooping) are captured by 1-2 DoF latent spaces.

Paper: [Learning Latent Actions to Control Assistive Robots](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8335729/) (2021)

#### 2I. RoLD -- Multi-task Manipulation Policy with Visuomotor Latent Diffusion (2024)

- Uses a trajectory latent autoencoder that compresses action sequences into low-dimensional latent representations.
- Demonstrates that action data can be condensed into a latent space with "strong skill-relevant semantics."

Paper: [Multi-task Manipulation Policy Modeling with Visuomotor Latent Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07312) (2024)

---

### TOPIC 3: Recent Concurrent Work (2025-2026)

#### 3A. VLS: Vision-Language Steering (Feb 2026, arXiv 2602.03973)

- **Training-free** inference-time adaptation of frozen diffusion/flow-matching robot policies.
- Treats adaptation as an inference-time control problem: steers the denoising sampling process using VLM-derived rewards.
- 31% improvement on CALVIN, 13% on LIBERO-PRO, real-world Franka deployment.
- Closely related to GSF: both modify the inference process of frozen generative policies without retraining.

Paper: [VLS: Steering Pretrained Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03973) (Feb 2026)

#### 3B. General Policy Composition (GPC) (Oct 2025, arXiv 2510.01068)

- Training-free method composing distributional scores of multiple diffusion/flow-matching policies via convex combination at test time.
- Proves that convex composition of scores yields a superior one-step functional objective; uses Gronwall-type bound to show improvement propagates through generation.
- Works across heterogeneous policy types (VA, VLA, diffusion, flow-matching).

Paper: [Compose Your Policies!](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01068) (Oct 2025)

#### 3C. Generative Predictive Control (GPC) (Feb 2025, arXiv 2502.00622)

- Inference-time enhancement of frozen diffusion policies via predictive world modeling.
- Generates multiple action proposals, ranks/refines them using a learned world model.
- GPC-RANK+OPT achieves ~15-25% gains over pure behavior cloning.

Paper: [Inference-Time Enhancement via Predictive World Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00622) (2025)

#### 3D. Dream Diffusion Policy (DDP) (March 2026, arXiv 2603.21017)

- Co-optimizes diffusion policy with diffusion world model via shared 3D encoder.
- Uses "real-imagination discrepancy" to detect OOD events; switches to world-model-conditioned imagination during disruptions.
- **73.8% OOD success** vs 23.9% baseline on MetaWorld; **83.3% vs 3.3%** in real-world spatial shifts.

Paper: [Dreaming the Unseen: World Model-regularized Diffusion Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21017) (March 2026)

#### 3E. RobustVLA (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.00037)

- "On Robustness of Vision-Language-Action Models against Multi-Modal Perturbations."
- Systematic evaluation of VLA model vulnerabilities under vision, language, and action perturbations.
- Provides RobustVLA benchmark/dataset for testing robotic policy robustness.

Paper: [On Robustness of VLA Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00037) (ICLR 2026)

#### 3F. FlowPolicy (AAAI 2025 Oral, arXiv 2412.04987)

- Consistency flow matching for robot manipulation achieving 7x inference speedup.
- Enables single-step inference while maintaining competitive success rates.

Paper: [FlowPolicy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04987) (AAAI 2025 Oral)

#### 3G. Mask World Model (April 2026, arXiv 2604.19683)

- Uses video diffusion to predict semantic mask evolution (geometric information bottleneck).
- 98.3% on LIBERO, 68.3% on RLBench, 67.5% on real Franka.

Paper: [Mask World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19683) (April 2026)

---

**For the bias-variance argument (Topic 1)**:
The strongest theoretical support comes from combining Kimura (2024) Theorem 3.3 (optimal weights require inverse covariance, not uniform weights) with Chen et al. Together, these establish that low-rank/low-frequency spectral structure is a fundamental property of robot action spaces, not just image domains.

**For concurrent work (Topic 3)**:
VLS (Feb 2026) and GPC/Compose Your Policies (Oct 2025) are the most closely related concurrent works -- both perform inference-time modification of frozen diffusion/flow-matching policies. ## RESEARCH FINDINGS REPORT

---

### TOPIC 1: Bias-Variance Decomposition for Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) Methods

I found several highly relevant papers that provide formal theoretical foundations you can use to argue that selective consensus (GSF) outperforms simple averaging (TTA).

#### 1A. "Understanding Test-Time Augmentation" -- Kimura (2024)

This is the most directly relevant paper. It provides:

- **Theorem 3.1**: The expected error of TTA is bounded from above by the average error of individual predictions. TTA cannot perform worse than the average individual model when the transformation class contains the identity.
- **Theorem 3.2**: When individual errors have zero mean and are uncorrelated, TTA achieves a factor-of-m improvement: R_TTA = (1/m) * R_avg. This is the best case for uniform averaging.
- **Proposition 2 (Ambiguity Decomposition)**: The TTA error decomposes as: R_TTA = [weighted average of individual errors] - [ambiguity term]. The ambiguity term measures prediction diversity. *Higher ambiguity (diverse predictions) benefits TTA; correlated predictions provide minimal gains.* This is critical for your argument -- if some dimensions have low ambiguity (high correlation across augmentations), averaging them adds noise without reducing error.
- **Theorem 3.3 (Optimal Weights)**: The closed-form optimal weights use the inverse covariance matrix of prediction errors: w_i = (sum_j Gamma^{-1}_{ij}) / (sum_k sum_j Gamma^{-1}_{kj}). The authors note the correlation matrix among augmented predictions is often near-singular, making uniform weights suboptimal. This directly supports dimension-wise weighting.

**Key argument for GSF**: Theorem 3.3 shows optimal aggregation requires *non-uniform* weights determined by the error covariance structure. GSF's dimension-selective consensus can be seen as a sparse approximation of this optimal weighting -- averaging only in dimensions where the ambiguity term is large (high sensitivity) and preserving the original prediction in dimensions where augmentations are redundant.

Paper: [Understanding Test-Time Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06892)

#### 1B. "Better Aggregation in Test-Time Augmentation" -- Shanmugam et al. (ICCV 2021)

Key findings:
- Even when TTA produces a net improvement, it changes many correct predictions into incorrect ones. Uniform averaging is demonstrably suboptimal.
- They propose a *learned weighting matrix* for aggregating TTA predictions that minimizes validation loss.
- Consistent improvements over uniform averaging across diverse models, datasets, and augmentations.

This empirically validates that dimension-wise or sample-wise selective aggregation beats uniform averaging.

Paper: [Better Aggregation in Test-Time Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.11156) (ICCV 2021)

#### 1C. "A Group-Theoretic Framework for Data Augmentation" -- Chen, Dobriban, Lee (JMLR 2020, NeurIPS 2020)

Key theoretical results:
- Data augmentation is formally equivalent to **averaging over group orbits**, which reduces variance.
- **Invariance-variance tradeoff**: Orbit averaging reduces variance, but introduces bias when the true function is not exactly invariant. The bias term vanishes under exact invariance.
- **Formal result**: The bias of the augmented estimator equals the original bias, and the covariance matrix *decreases in the Loewner order*, hence MSE decreases.

**Key argument for GSF**: This framework shows that averaging helps *only along directions where the function has approximate invariance*. In dimensions where the function is NOT invariant to the augmentation group, averaging introduces bias. GSF's selective consensus naturally restricts averaging to dimensions with approximate invariance (low geometric sensitivity), avoiding the bias penalty in non-invariant dimensions.

Paper: [A Group-Theoretic Framework for Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10905) (JMLR Vol 21, 2020)

#### 1D. "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly Sides of Data Augmentation" -- Lin et al. (JMLR 2024)

Key findings:
- DA induces *implicit spectral regularization* through two effects: (1) manipulating relative eigenvalue proportions of the data covariance matrix, and (2) uniformly boosting the entire spectrum (equivalent to ridge regression).
- Demonstrates that augmentation can *hurt* in certain regimes ("the ugly side"), particularly when the spectral manipulation misaligns with the signal structure.
- The framework reveals discrepancies between overparameterized and underparameterized regimes.

**Key argument for GSF**: This paper shows augmentation's benefit depends on alignment between the augmentation's spectral effect and the signal's spectral structure. In robot action spaces where different dimensions have different spectral properties, uniform augmentation/averaging across all dimensions creates spectral misalignment. GSF's dimension-selective approach avoids this.

Paper: [The Good, the Bad and the Ugly Sides of Data Augmentation](https://jmlr.org/papers/v25/22-1312.html) (JMLR Vol 25, 2024)

#### 1E. "Efficient Improvement of Classification Accuracy via Selective Test-Time Augmentation" (Information Sciences, 2023)

Proposes selective TTA that quantifies predictive uncertainty to determine *whether* TTA should be performed, applying it only when uncertainty is high. This reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy. Selective aggregation based on risk/reward criteria reduces bias from abnormal transformations.

Paper: [Selective Test-Time Augmentation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0020025523007338) (Information Sciences, 2023)

---

### TOPIC 2: Spectral Structure in Robot Action Spaces

I found strong evidence that robot action spaces exhibit spectral structure (low-rank, low-frequency dominance), drawn from ROBOTICS domains rather than images.

#### 2A. FreqPolicy -- (2025, arXiv 2506.01583)

This is the strongest single paper for your needs. It provides direct empirical analysis of spectral structure in robot action spaces:

- **Key finding**: The first 30% of frequency bands preserves 95% of signal energy in robot actions.
- Most energy concentrates in the 0-10% low-frequency bands across both high-DoF (26-DoF Adroit hand) and low-DoF (10-DoF Robomimic gripper) tasks.
- Simple tasks (pick-and-place) maintain performance with only 12% of low-frequency content preserved.
- Complex dexterous tasks require more frequency components.
- "Low-frequency components reflect global movement patterns, while high-frequency components encode fine local details."
- Uses Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) analysis on Adroit and Robomimic benchmarks.

**This directly supports the GSF assumption** that robot action spaces have spectral structure where different frequency bands carry different amounts of information.

Paper: [FreqPolicy: Frequency Autoregressive Visuomotor Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01583) (2025)

#### 2B. Santello, Flanders, Soechting -- "Postural Hand Synergies for Tool Use" (J. Neuroscience, 1998)

The landmark paper on hand synergies:
- PCA of 15 hand joint angles during grasping shows the **first 2 principal components explain >80% of variance**.
- Higher-order components are not random noise but carry object-specific information.
- This is a foundational result showing low-rank structure in manipulation-relevant action spaces.

Paper: [Postural Hand Synergies for Tool Use](https://www.jneurosci.org/content/18/23/10105) (J. Neuroscience, 1998)

#### 2C. PCHands -- PCA-based Hand Pose Synergy Representation (2025, arXiv 2508.07945)

- Demonstrates that **2 principal components are typically sufficient** for learning complex dexterous manipulation tasks on hands with 16, 9, and 18 DoF.
- The first principal component universally encodes hand opening/closing across all 16 tested manipulator morphologies.
- Performance with 1-2 PCs was "predominantly better than 4-pc" in demonstration-augmented learning.

Paper: [PCHands: PCA-based Hand Pose Synergy Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07945) (2025)

#### 2D. PCA-Based Algorithms for Humanoid Robot Motion Behavior (Int. J. Humanoid Robotics, 2015)

- Uses PCA to find synergies in humanoid robot motion.
- Demonstrates that robot motion trajectories can be efficiently represented using a small number of principal components.

Paper: [PCA-Based Algorithms to Find Synergies for Humanoid Robot Motion](https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0219843615500371)

#### 2E. "Exploiting Upper-Limb Functional Principal Components" (Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 2020)

Directly relevant empirical results:
- **More than 80% of variance explained by only 3 functional principal components** for robot arm trajectories.
- The first component alone accounts for 96% of cost reduction in trajectory optimization.
- Free-motion tasks need only 1 PC; single-obstacle scenarios need 2; double-obstacle needs 3.
- Lower-order PCs contribute low-frequency motion, higher-order PCs add high-frequency detail -- directly paralleling the frequency-domain analysis in FreqPolicy.

Paper: [Exploiting Upper-Limb Functional Principal Components](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7218840/) (2020)

#### 2F. EigenTrajectory -- Low-Rank Descriptors for Multi-Modal Trajectory Forecasting (ICCV 2023)

- Uses SVD decomposition on trajectory data, demonstrating strong low-rank structure.
- **k=6 eigenvectors** effectively represent trajectory space (originally 2*T dimensional).
- First two eigenvectors encode constant-velocity motion; subsequent ones capture velocity changes and fine details.
- Eigenvalue spectrum shows rapid decay, confirming low-rank structure.

Paper: [EigenTrajectory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09306) (ICCV 2023)

#### 2G. Dimensionality Reduction for Probabilistic Movement Primitives (2015)

- The intrinsic dimensionality of human/robot movements is small compared to the number of DoF.
- Dimensionality reduction applied to ProMPs preserves essential trajectory information.

Paper: [Dimensionality Reduction for Probabilistic Movement Primitives](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/283882361_Dimensionality_reduction_for_probabilistic_movement_primitives) (2015)

#### 2H. "Learning Latent Actions to Control Assistive Robots" (Autonomous Robots, 2021)

- Demonstrates that 7-DoF robot arm control can be compressed to **1-2 latent dimensions** while preserving task-relevant structure.
- Even complex manipulation tasks (reaching, cutting, scooping) are captured by 1-2 DoF latent spaces.

Paper: [Learning Latent Actions to Control Assistive Robots](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8335729/) (2021)

#### 2I. RoLD -- Multi-task Manipulation Policy with Visuomotor Latent Diffusion (2024)

- Uses a trajectory latent autoencoder that compresses action sequences into low-dimensional latent representations.
- Demonstrates that action data can be condensed into a latent space with "strong skill-relevant semantics."

Paper: [Multi-task Manipulation Policy Modeling with Visuomotor Latent Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07312) (2024)

---

### TOPIC 3: Recent Concurrent Work (2025-2026)

#### 3A. VLS: Vision-Language Steering (Feb 2026, arXiv 2602.03973)

- **Training-free** inference-time adaptation of frozen diffusion/flow-matching robot policies.
- Treats adaptation as an inference-time control problem: steers the denoising sampling process using VLM-derived rewards.
- 31% improvement on CALVIN, 13% on LIBERO-PRO, real-world Franka deployment.
- Closely related to GSF: both modify the inference process of frozen generative policies without retraining.

Paper: [VLS: Steering Pretrained Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03973) (Feb 2026)

#### 3B. General Policy Composition (GPC) (Oct 2025, arXiv 2510.01068)

- Training-free method composing distributional scores of multiple diffusion/flow-matching policies via convex combination at test time.
- Proves that convex composition of scores yields a superior one-step functional objective; uses Gronwall-type bound to show improvement propagates through generation.
- Works across heterogeneous policy types (VA, VLA, diffusion, flow-matching).

Paper: [Compose Your Policies!](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01068) (Oct 2025)

#### 3C. Generative Predictive Control (GPC) (Feb 2025, arXiv 2502.00622)

- Inference-time enhancement of frozen diffusion policies via predictive world modeling.
- Generates multiple action proposals, ranks/refines them using a learned world model.
- GPC-RANK+OPT achieves ~15-25% gains over pure behavior cloning.

Paper: [Inference-Time Enhancement via Predictive World Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00622) (2025)

#### 3D. Dream Diffusion Policy (DDP) (March 2026, arXiv 2603.21017)

- Co-optimizes diffusion policy with diffusion world model via shared 3D encoder.
- Uses "real-imagination discrepancy" to detect OOD events; switches to world-model-conditioned imagination during disruptions.
- **73.8% OOD success** vs 23.9% baseline on MetaWorld; **83.3% vs 3.3%** in real-world spatial shifts.

Paper: [Dreaming the Unseen: World Model-regularized Diffusion Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21017) (March 2026)

#### 3E. RobustVLA (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.00037)

- "On Robustness of Vision-Language-Action Models against Multi-Modal Perturbations."
- Systematic evaluation of VLA model vulnerabilities under vision, language, and action perturbations.
- Provides RobustVLA benchmark/dataset for testing robotic policy robustness.

Paper: [On Robustness of VLA Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00037) (ICLR 2026)

#### 3F. FlowPolicy (AAAI 2025 Oral, arXiv 2412.04987)

- Consistency flow matching for robot manipulation achieving 7x inference speedup.
- Enables single-step inference while maintaining competitive success rates.

Paper: [FlowPolicy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04987) (AAAI 2025 Oral)

#### 3G. Mask World Model (April 2026, arXiv 2604.19683)

- Uses video diffusion to predict semantic mask evolution (geometric information bottleneck).
- 98.3% on LIBERO, 68.3% on RLBench, 67.5% on real Franka.

Paper: [Mask World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19683) (April 2026)

---

### SYNTHESIS: Key Arguments for Your Proposal Revision

**For the bias-variance argument (Topic 1)**:
The strongest theoretical support comes from combining Kimura (2024) Theorem 3.3 (optimal weights require inverse covariance, not uniform weights) with Chen et al. (JMLR 2020) (averaging helps only along invariant directions, introduces bias otherwise) and Lin et al. (JMLR 2024) (augmentation can hurt when spectral effects misalign with signal structure). Together, these establish that: (1) uniform averaging is provably suboptimal when prediction errors are correlated; (2) averaging introduces bias in non-invariant dimensions; (3) the benefit depends on alignment between augmentation structure and signal spectrum. GSF's dimension-selective consensus naturally addresses all three issues.

**For the spectral structure argument (Topic 2)**:
FreqPolicy (2025) is the strongest direct evidence from robot action domains: 95% of energy in the first 30% of frequency bands, tested on Adroit (26-DoF) and Robomimic (10-DoF). This can be supplemented with Santello (1998) showing 2 PCs capture >80% of grasp variance, the upper-limb PCA paper showing 3 PCs capture >80% of arm trajectory variance, PCHands (2025) showing 2 PCs suffice for dexterous manipulation, and EigenTrajectory (2023) showing k=6 SVD components represent trajectory spaces. Together, these establish that low-rank/low-frequency spectral structure is a fundamental property of robot action spaces, not just image domains.

**For concurrent work (Topic 3)**:
VLS (Feb 2026) and GPC/Compose Your Policies (Oct 2025) are the most closely related concurrent works -- both perform inference-time modification of frozen diffusion/flow-matching policies. DDP (March 2026) is also relevant for its geometric robustness approach. Position GSF as complementary: these methods modify the sampling process or compose multiple policies, while GSF provides a lightweight post-hoc consensus filter that requires no world model, no VLM, and no additional policy.

  "approach": "We propose Geometric Sensitivity Filtering (GSF), a training-free inference-time method that improves geometric robustness of pre-trained flow-matching/diffusion robot policies by decomposing velocity fields into geometrically-stable and geometrically-sensitive subspaces, then selectively applying augmentation consensus in the sensitive subspace while preserving nominal precision in the stable subspace.

**Key Theoretical Insight: Why This Differs From Ensemble Methods.** Flow-matching velocity fields v_θ(a_t, t | o) are deterministic functions: given a fixed noisy action a_t at integration step t with observation o, the output is a single vector with no stochasticity. This means that when we compute velocity fields from geometrically-augmented observations {T_k(o)}, ALL variance across the K augmented velocity fields is attributable to geometric sensitivity — there is no multi-modality confound. This distinguishes GSF from ensemble/disagreement methods (e.g., Diff-DAgger shows ensemble variance conflates multi-modality with uncertainty at the trajectory level). At the velocity-field level with fixed (a_t, t), the analysis is clean.

**Formal Bias-Variance Argument: Why GSF Dominates Simple TTA.** We frame the comparison as a bias-variance decomposition grounded in TTA optimality theory. Let v*(a_t, t) denote the ideal velocity (what the policy would predict under training-distribution geometry). Under geometric perturbation, the nominal velocity v_0 = v_θ(a_t, t | o_perturbed) has: low bias in geometrically-stable dimensions (these are approximately invariant to the perturbation by definition), but high variance/error in geometrically-sensitive dimensions (these change substantially with the perturbation). The TTA mean v̄ = (1/K)Σ v_k has: reduced variance everywhere (by averaging), but introduces bias in stable dimensions because it averages over augmented observations that don't match the actual scene — as Chen et al. (JMLR 2020) prove, averaging introduces bias in directions where the function is NOT invariant to the augmentation group.

GSF achieves the best of both: v_0 in stable dimensions (low bias from near-invariance, no averaging bias) and v̄ in sensitive dimensions (averaging reduces the perturbation-induced error, and any averaging bias is smaller than the perturbation-induced error it replaces). This is not ad hoc: Kimura (2024, Theorem 3.3) proves the optimal TTA aggregation weights are determined by the inverse covariance matrix of prediction errors. GSF's SVD-based decomposition provides a non-parametric approximation of this optimal weighting: dimensions with high covariance (high sensitivity) receive averaging (high weight on consensus), while dimensions with low covariance (low sensitivity) retain the nominal prediction (zero weight on consensus). The key assumption: v_0's perturbation-induced error in sensitive directions exceeds v̄'s averaging bias in those same directions. This holds when the perturbation is large relative to the augmentation range — precisely the regime where robustness is needed.

**Addressing the Augmentation-Perturbation Magnitude Gap.** GSF uses small augmentations (±2-8° rotation, ±2-5% translation) to probe local sensitivity, while LIBERO-Plus camera perturbations can be substantially larger (C2: 15-75° azimuth/elevation shifts; C1: 1.01-2.00x distance; C3: 2-10° orientation). The critical claim is that GSF needs only DIRECTIONAL accuracy — identifying WHICH velocity dimensions are geometrically sensitive — not MAGNITUDE accuracy. This is supported by: (1) The singular-vector alignment theorem (arXiv:2602.12384, Theorem 6.1), which proves that dominant singular vectors of the Jacobian converge to a shared basis under spectral separation, meaning sensitivity DIRECTIONS are structurally determined by network weights and approximately invariant to perturbation magnitude. (2) Empirical evidence from Beyond Activation Alignment (arXiv:2605.03222) showing local sensitivity directions transfer to finite perturbation regimes. (3) Phase 0 includes an explicit diagnostic: compute SVD at three augmentation magnitudes (small: ±2°, medium: ±5°, large: ±10°) and measure cosine similarity of top eigenvectors across magnitudes. If cosine similarity > 0.8, directional invariance holds; if < 0.5, the method's theoretical basis is weakened and augmentation magnitude becomes a critical hyperparameter requiring task-specific tuning.

Furthermore, augmentation magnitude is included as a key Phase 2 hyperparameter sweep (±2°, ±4°, ±6°, ±8°) to empirically determine the optimal probing range. Since LIBERO-Plus L1-L5 levels are defined by model performance rather than perturbation magnitude, the relevant question is inherently about which geometric dimensions matter — exactly what GSF's directional decomposition targets.

**Phased Research Plan with Explicit Gates:**

**Phase 0 — Spectral and Directional Diagnostic (1 day, ~2-3h H100).** Before committing to full development: take 5-10 LIBERO-Plus camera-perturbed episodes, compute velocity fields from 8 small geometric augmentations at several integration steps. Two diagnostics: (a) Eigenvalue spectrum analysis — compute the covariance of augmented velocity fields and examine eigenvalue decay. GATE: If the spectrum is flat (ratio of top to bottom eigenvalue < 3), there is no exploitable structure and GSF cannot work — abort. If there is a clear spectral gap (top 2-3 eigenvalues dominate, >10x ratio), proceed. (b) Directional invariance test — repeat the eigenvalue analysis at three augmentation magnitudes (±2°, ±5°, ±10°) and compute pairwise cosine similarity of the top-3 eigenvectors. GATE: If average cosine similarity < 0.5, sensitivity directions are magnitude-dependent and the augmentation-perturbation gap is a fundamental limitation — downgrade to augmentation-magnitude sweep only. Expected outcome: based on evidence from robot action space spectral structure (FreqPolicy: 95% energy in first 30% of frequency bands; PCA studies: 2-3 PCs capture >80% of manipulation variance) and singular-vector alignment theory, we expect both spectral gap and directional stability — but this must be verified empirically.

**Phase 2 — GSF Implementation and Evaluation (7-10 days, with internal gate).**

**Core Mechanism.** At each integration step t during inference:
1. Given current observation o and noisy action a_t, compute the nominal velocity: v_0 = v_θ(a_t, t | o)
2. Generate K=4-6 small geometric augmentations of the observation: {T_k(o)} where T_k are random camera jitter (±2-8° rotation, ±2-5% translation) and/or spatial crops
3. Compute augmented velocities: v_k = v_θ(a_t, t | T_k(o)) for k=1,...,K
4. Compute velocity covariance across augmentations: C_t = (1/K) Σ_k (v_k - v̄)(v_k - v̄)^T where v̄ = (1/K)Σ v_k
5. SVD of C_t = U_t Λ_t U_t^T. Top eigenvectors (high eigenvalues) = high geometric sensitivity directions
6. Construct subspace decomposition: Π_high = Σ_{i: λ_i > τ·tr(Λ)} u_i u_i^T, Π_low = I - Π_high
7. Apply selective consensus: v_filtered = Π_low · v_0 + Π_high · v̄
8. Use v_filtered for the integration step

**Interpretation:** In low-sensitivity directions (Π_low), we trust the nominal velocity v_0 — these components are approximately invariant to geometric perturbation, so the nominal prediction retains full precision without averaging bias (Chen et al. JMLR 2020). In high-sensitivity directions (Π_high), we replace the unreliable nominal with the augmentation consensus v̄ — which averages out geometric-sensitivity-induced variability, providing a more robust estimate. This implements a sparse approximation of the optimal TTA weights from Kimura (2024, Theorem 3.3).

**Phase 2 Internal Gate — GSF vs. Simple TTA Decision Point (after ~day 8-9).** After running GSF and simple TTA on Camera L1 (the easiest geometric perturbation condition) with 20 episodes: If GSF's advantage over simple TTA > 3pp → proceed with full evaluation across all conditions. If GSF's advantage is 1-3pp → marginal; complete evaluation but prepare dual framing (method + analysis). If GSF's advantage < 1pp → pivot to ANALYSIS contribution: characterize WHAT the sensitive dimensions encode via eigenvector visualization, analyze WHETHER simple TTA's uniform averaging is already near-optimal for this setting, and report the finding that velocity-field spectral structure exists but selective consensus provides limited marginal benefit over uniform consensus — this transforms a negative method result into a positive analytical insight about geometric sensitivity structure in flow-matching robot policies. This pivot produces a valuable contribution: the first characterization of velocity-field sensitivity structure under geometric perturbation, the demonstration that TTA helps flow policies (confirming VOTE-style findings at the velocity level), and empirical testing of TTA optimality theory (Kimura 2024) in the robot policy setting.

**Adaptive Integration Schedule.** Early integration steps (high noise/far from data) determine coarse trajectory structure and are most geometry-dependent; later steps refine timing and precision. Apply GSF with adaptive strength: aggressive decomposition (lower τ, larger Π_high) at early steps, conservative (higher τ, smaller Π_high) at later steps. Apply full GSF at steps 1-4 (of 10) and nominal-only at steps 5-10, with linear interpolation for the threshold.

**Computational Overhead.** GSF requires K+1 forward passes per filtered integration step. For K=4, applying GSF at M=4 of T=10 steps: 4×5 + 6×1 = 26 forward passes vs. 10 baseline — 2.6x overhead. Optimizations: (i) Cache visual backbone features across integration steps (the observation doesn't change; only recompute action-expert forward pass). (ii) For Fast-WAM's MoT architecture, the video DiT backbone (5B) is shared; only the 1B action expert needs K+1 passes. With feature caching, effective overhead is ~1.5-2x on wall-clock time.

Secondary: Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., diffusion-based, widely used). Extension: demonstrate on a non-WAM architecture (e.g., standard Diffusion Policy or a VLA with diffusion/flow head) to validate architecture-agnosticism.

**Evaluation Strategy.** Primary benchmark: LIBERO-Plus geometric perturbations — Camera (L1, L3) and Robot-Init (L1, L3), plus Light as control (non-geometric, expect no benefit or slight degradation). Standard LIBERO as sanity check (expect 1-3% degradation from information loss in filtered components).

Baselines: (i) Fast-WAM standard inference (nominal only), (ii) Fast-WAM + Simple TTA: average K+1 velocity fields uniformly then integrate (same compute budget as GSF — the critical apples-to-apples comparison), (iii) Fast-WAM + VOTE-style action voting: generate K+1 full trajectories and select by consensus, (iv) Fast-WAM + GSF (ours — selective consensus in sensitivity-decomposed subspace).

**Framing vs. Competitors:** GSF is positioned as a lightweight inference-time method for improving geometric robustness of pre-trained flow/diffusion policies, complementary to training-time approaches.
